finding.claim: Missing authentication on POST /settings/email: the handler uses @login_optional instead of @login_required, so unauthenticated requests reach set_email with g.uid = None. Its sibling /settings/password correctly uses @login_required. An unauthenticated attacker can trigger an account email change, and if set_email treats a None uid as a match, could affect an unintended account. This also enables account-takeover via email change and password reset.
finding.source: Unauthenticated HTTP POST to /settings/email with no session cookie
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37, a state-changing account operation

trace.note: @login_optional applied, so no abort(401) when the session has no uid
g.uid = session.get('uid') evaluates to None for anonymous callers and the request continues
set_email(g.uid, ...) is called with uid None; no ownership or auth check

finding.guards_checked: login_required is not applied (compare routes.py:42 on /settings/password, which has it). There is no in-handler uid check, no CSRF token, and no re-authentication. login_optional never aborts. set_email is a stub (routes.py:48), so the behaviour with uid=None cannot be confirmed. The missing authentication guard is still clear.

verdict.guard_found: none (login_optional at routes.py:19-25 never aborts; no in-handler uid check, no CSRF)
verdict.reason: routes.py:35 applies @login_optional, which sets g.uid=None without aborting (routes.py:22), so an anonymous POST reaches set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37, unlike /settings/password's @login_required (routes.py:42, abort at :12); set_email is a stub (routes.py:48), so the real impact depends on its implementation, but the missing auth guard is real.
